name: Silozi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Lynn, Celinah Leboela. 2008. Comparative analysis of the phonology of Silozi and Sesotho. MA dissertation (Linguistic Science), University of Zambia. 104 pp. UNZA DSpace item 123456789/1122. The Lozi-specific rule is reported there from Jalla, Adolphe. 1937. Elementary grammar of the Lozi language. London: USCL, and Mwisiya, M. W. 1977. Introduction to Silozi grammar. Lusaka: NECZAM (both unreachable).
catalog_locator: Section 3.17.4 'Length and Stress', thesis pp. 62-63; pages read directly.
catalog_quote: What is commonly referred to as stress, accent or emphasis, which may be accompanied by gestures of various kinds, is achieved by a combination of a high or low toneme plus length on the same syllable, usually the penultimate syllable. Both languages under study share these prosodic features. ... While Jalla (1937) on the Lozi, contends that as a rule, accent is on the penultimate syllable as in: musebezi (work) ... Jalla says the same applies to monosyllables, with the exception of /ca/ when it means /to eat/. A monosyllable at the end of a sentence has no accent, the accent being on the syllable preceding it as in /ha ba si ka ta/ - (they have not come); /i la ca/ - (it will burn); Exceptionally, the accent may be on the last syllable as in: /mulenen/ (the Capital) ... /nahen/ (in the veld) ... There are however some exceptions to this general rule. Mwisiya (1977) says: (a) In a command the last syllable is lengthened: as in: kuze:ni! (keep quiet!) Zama:ya! (Go!) (b) In a question the penultimate syllable is not lengthened: as in: Wa zamaya?(Are you going?); U zwa kai? (Where do you come from?);

new_statements.locator: Section 3.17.4 'Length and Stress', pp. 62-63 (pp. 74-75 of UNZA item 123456789/1122)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (104-page scan-only scan, no text) is held with /MD5SUMS. I rendered pp. 74-75 (= thesis pp. 62-63) to images and read them directly, independent of the saved scanned. Every fragment of the reported quote is on those pages verbatim; the ellipses elide only the Westermann & Ward / Doke / Cole discussion, the Sesotho comparanda '(mosebetsi in Sesotho.. from /z/->ts/)' and '- /moreneng/ (Sotho equivalent)'. The only thing the plain-text quote cannot show is that the thesis bolds the accented syllable in the examples (muse-BE-zi, ha ba si KA ta, i LA ca, mulene-N, nahe-N, Wa zaMAya, U ZWA kai), which actually strengthens the penult reading. Locator 'Section 3.17.4 Length and Stress,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Silozi word accent (realised as tone plus vowel length, not dynamic stress) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; a sentence-final monosyllabic word is unaccented and the accent falls on the syllable before it (i.e. the penult of the phrase-final group).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described for Lozi (only Doke's general Bantu remark about secondary stresses at intervals is quoted).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic ca 'eat'; locative nouns in -n' (mulenen' 'at the capital', nahen' 'in the veld') with final accent; per Mwisiya 1977 the final syllable is lengthened in commands (Zamaya!) and the penult is not lengthened in questions (Wa zamaya?).
new_statements.domain_note: Accent = H/L tone + length on the penult; behaves phrase-penultimately with sentence-final monosyllables. Kashoki & Mann 1978 say Zambian languages have near-even stress with at most slight penult prominence tied to lengthening; modern tonal work (Yukawa 1987; Bickmore 2023; Bickmore & Riedel 2025) treats Silozi as a H/L tone language that has lost contrastive vowel length and bars pre-pausal H, and makes no stress statement. The Lozi-specific rule in Lynn is taken from Jalla 1937 and Mwisiya 1977 (primary sources not openly available).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe standard Silozi (glottocode lozi1239, ISO loz) of Zambia's Western Province (Mongu/Senanga/Lusaka speakers); Lynn 2008 treats Silozi comparatively with Sesotho and takes the Lozi-specific accent rule from Jalla 1937 (whose grammar describes the same language, earlier called Sikololo). No dialect split is at issue.

sources.note: Sec. 3.17.4 'Length and Stress' (pp. 61-65): stress/accent in Silozi and Sesotho = high or low toneme plus length on the same syllable, 'usually the penultimate syllable'; cites Jalla 1937 that Lozi accent is as a rule penultimate (musebezi), also on monosyllables except ca 'eat'; a sentence-final monosyllable is unaccented, accent falling on the syllable before it (ha ba si ka ta; i la ca); exceptionally final accent in locatives mulenen', nahen'; Mwisiya 1977: in commands the last syllable is lengthened, in questions the penult is not lengthened.

sources.citation: Kashoki, Mubanga E. & Michael Mann. 1978. A general sketch of the Bantu languages of Zambia. In Ohannessian & Kashoki (eds.), Language in Zambia, pp. 47-100. London: IAI. (UNZA DSpace text bundle)
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 Tone and Stress (pp. 70-71), generic for Zambian languages incl. Lozi: 'syllables are more or less evenly stressed'; in some languages the penultimate seems slightly more forceful, possibly an effect of penultimate lengthening; stress never distinguishes words; every syllable carries H or L tone (Lozi example given for tone). No Lozi-specific stress rule.

tone.summary: The abstract describes Silozi as a Bantu tone language with lexical High tones on subject markers, object markers and verb roots, an underlying High that shifts one TBU rightward and then doubles onto the next, OCP-driven High deletions, and grammatical (melodic) High tones that land on the penult or the ultima to mark TAM categories; eleven tonal rules are stated for infinitives and finite verbs.
